title: Status Codes and Failure Responses
learningObjectives: Explain the key ideas and terminology of status codes and failure responses.
Recognize how the concept is used in real software communication.
Identify common mistakes or risks associated with this topic.
Apply the concept to a small, fictional API scenario.
Review a communication design and justify appropriate choices.

understand.concept: HTTP status codes summarize response outcomes. Broad groups are 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client/request-related problems, and 5xx server failures. Common examples include 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content, 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized (authentication needed), 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 429 Too Many Requests, and 500 Internal Server Error. APIs may add structured error details.
understand.whyItMatters: Status codes help clients decide whether to display data, retry, request login, correct input, or report a failure.
understand.analogy: Think of a delivery process with a sender, a message, and a receiver who returns a confirmation or explanation.
understand.analogyLimit: Software communication may involve complex protocols, asynchronous timing, security, and partial failures that this everyday analogy cannot fully capture.

explain.narrative:
HTTP status codes summarize response outcomes. Broad groups are 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client/request-related problems, and 5xx server failures. Common examples include 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content, 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized (authentication needed), 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 429 Too Many Requests, and 500 Internal Server Error. APIs may add structured error details.

Use the protocol and service documentation as the authoritative guide for a real API. Examples here are conceptual and intentionally do not make live network calls.

examples.title: Distinguish forbidden
examples.explanation: 403 indicates the server understood but refuses the request.

examples.title: Handle not found
examples.explanation: 404 indicates the requested resource was not found.

examples.title: Identify throttling
examples.explanation: 429 signals too many requests and may include retry guidance.

commonMistakes: Assuming every request succeeds or returns the same shape.
Treating parsing as validation or authentication as authorization.
Ignoring timeout, rate-limit, and failure responses.
Embedding secret credentials in public client code.
Retrying operations without considering duplicate side effects.

guidedTask.title: Guided Practice
guidedTask.instructions: Create a response-handling table for a course API: 200, 201, 204, 400, 401, 403, 404, 429, and 500. For each, write a user-friendly action.
steps: Create a response-handling table for a course API: 200, 201, 204, 400, 401, 403, 404, 429, and 500. For each, write a user-friendly action.
Sketch the communication sequence and identify the client/server roles.
Define expected success and failure outcomes.
Choose checks, timeout or retry behavior where appropriate.
Review your design for privacy and safe handling.

independentTask.title: Independent Practice
independentTask.instructions: Write a client decision flow for status groups. Include when to display data, prompt login, show a validation error, back off/retry, or report a service issue.
requirements: Use a fictional or toy service; do not include live secrets.
Write a client decision flow for status groups. Include when to display data, prompt login, show a validation error, back off/retry, or report a service issue.
Document assumptions, edge cases, and how you would test them.

hints: 401 relates to authentication; 403 to permission refusal.
404 means the resource was not found.
429 may require waiting or honoring Retry-After.
5xx usually indicates server-side failure; avoid aggressive retry loops.
